moduleTitle: Creation: the Genesis accounts, the nature of God, human dignity and stewardship

note.specFocus: AQA 8062 Catholic Christianity, key beliefs: creation in Genesis 1 and 2; what the accounts show about the nature of God, the dignity of human beings (imago Dei) and humanity's relationship with creation (stewardship); different Christian interpretations of creation.
note.summary:
KEY IDEA: Catholics believe God freely created everything that exists out of nothing (ex nihilo, CCC 296). Creation was an act of love by the whole Trinity. They believe Genesis teaches religious truth about God, humanity and the world, not a scientific timetable.

GENESIS 1 (1:1–2:4a): God creates in six "days" by his word: "Let there be light". The order runs from light, sky, land and plants to the sun and moon, then sea creatures and birds, then land animals, and finally human beings. After each stage "God saw that it was good". At the end it was "very good" (1:31). Humans are made "in the image of God… male and female he created them" (1:26–27) and told to "be fruitful and multiply… and have dominion" (1:28). God rests on the seventh day, which is the root of the Sabbath.
What it shows about God: God is omnipotent (creates by word alone), transcendent (beyond creation), orderly, good and the source of all life. The Spirit "sweeping over the waters" (1:2) and "Let us make" (1:26) are read as hints of the Trinity. John 1:1–3 adds that all things were made through the Word (the Son).

GENESIS 2 (2:4b–25): A more personal account. God forms the man from "the dust of the ground" and breathes "the breath of life" into his nostrils (2:7). He places him in the Garden of Eden "to till it and keep it" (2:15). Adam names the animals. God forms the woman from the man's rib, because "it is not good that the man should be alone" (2:18). What it shows: God is immanent and personal, involved closely with his creation. Humans are both physical (dust) and spiritual (God's breath, the soul). Humans are made for relationship and marriage.

HUMAN DIGNITY: Being made in God's image (imago Dei) means every human being has dignity, reason, free will and the ability to love and know God (CCC 356–357). "The human person… is not just something, but someone." This underpins Catholic teaching on the sanctity of life, equality of men and women, and human rights.

STEWARDSHIP: "Dominion" does not mean exploitation. Humans are stewards, caretakers responsible to God for the world (CCC 373, 2415). Pope Francis's encyclical Laudato Si' (2015) says the Bible gives no basis for "tyrannical anthropocentrism". It calls for "ecological conversion" and care for "our common home". Catholics respond through recycling and energy projects in parishes, CAFOD climate campaigns and the annual Season of Creation (1 September – 4 October).

DIFFERENT CHRISTIAN VIEWS:
• Literalist or fundamentalist Christians (some evangelicals, "Young Earth" creationists) believe Genesis is a literal historical account: six 24-hour days, a world only thousands of years old.
• The Catholic Church teaches that Genesis uses "figurative language" (CCC 390) to express real truths. It is "true" without being a science textbook. Pope Pius XII (Humani Generis, 1950) allowed study of evolution as long as the soul is understood to be directly created by God. Pope John Paul II (1996) said evolution is "more than a hypothesis".
• Many Catholics and other Christians accept the Big Bang theory and theistic evolution: God works through natural processes. The Big Bang was first proposed by Fr Georges Lemaître, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist (1927).
• Some Christians support Intelligent Design, arguing that complexity in nature points to a designer.

KEY TERMS: creation ex nihilo, omnipotent, transcendent, immanent, imago Dei, stewardship, dominion, literalism, theistic evolution, Laudato Si'.

questions.question:
In Genesis 2, from what does God form the first man?
A) Water from a river
B) A rib
C) The dust of the ground
D) Light
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: C) The dust of the ground.

Genesis 2:7: 'the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life'. The rib (B) is used to form the woman (Genesis 2:21–22).
questions.examTip: Know the details of both accounts. Examiners can test the difference between Genesis 1 (word, six days) and Genesis 2 (dust, breath, garden, rib).

questions.question:
Which term means that God created the universe 'out of nothing'?
A) Ex nihilo
B) Imago Dei
C) Agape
D) Magisterium
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: A) Ex nihilo.

Ex nihilo is Latin for 'out of nothing' (CCC 296). Imago Dei means 'image of God'. Agape is selfless love. The Magisterium is the teaching authority of the Church.
questions.examTip: Latin key terms come up often. Make a glossary card for each one.

questions.question: Give one thing that the Genesis creation accounts show about the nature of God.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one from:
• God is omnipotent (creates simply by speaking)
• God is creator of everything / creates out of nothing
• God is good (everything was 'very good')
• God is transcendent, beyond and before creation
• God is personal or immanent (breathes life into Adam, walks in the garden)
• God is a God of order
questions.examTip: One clear attribute is enough. 'Omnipotent' or 'creator' is fine.

questions.question: Give one meaning of the Catholic belief that humans are made 'in the image of God'.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one from:
• Every human being has dignity and sacred value
• Humans have reason and free will
• Humans have a soul / can have a relationship with God
• Humans can love and be creative
• Male and female are equal in dignity (Genesis 1:27)
questions.examTip: Avoid saying humans 'look like' God physically. Catholic teaching is about spiritual qualities and dignity.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief that humans are made in the image of God influences Catholics today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Catholics believe every human life is sacred from conception to natural death (1 mark). Because every person reflects God's image, Catholics oppose abortion and euthanasia, and many support hospices and pregnancy-support charities (2nd mark).

Second way: Catholics treat all people as equal in dignity regardless of race, sex, wealth or disability (1 mark). Genesis 1:27 says God made humans 'male and female', both in his image. This motivates Catholics to challenge discrimination and to support refugees and the poor through groups such as CAFOD and the SVP. CST teaches that human dignity is the foundation of all social justice (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Make each development show what Catholics do as a result of the belief. That is what 'influence' means.

questions.question: Explain two different Christian views about how the Genesis creation accounts should be understood.
questions.modelAnswer:
First view: Some Christians, such as fundamentalist evangelicals or 'Young Earth' creationists, read Genesis literally (1 mark). They believe God created the world in six 24-hour days only a few thousand years ago. They reject evolution because the Bible is the inerrant word of God and should be taken at face value (2nd mark).

Second view: The Catholic Church teaches that Genesis uses symbolic or figurative language to express religious truths (1 mark). It is true about who created the world and why, not about how or when. Catholics can therefore accept the Big Bang (first proposed by the Catholic priest Georges Lemaître) and evolution, provided God is understood as creator and the human soul as directly given by God (CCC 390; Humani Generis) (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Make sure the two views genuinely differ, for example literal versus symbolic, and develop each one with a reason or example.

questions.question:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the role of human beings in creation.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First belief: Humans are stewards of creation (1 mark). God put Adam in the garden 'to till it and keep it' (Genesis 2:15), so humans are responsible to God for caring for the earth. They do not own it outright, and they will be accountable for how they treat the environment and animals (CCC 2415) (2nd mark).

Second belief: Humans are the high point of creation and have a unique dignity (1 mark). They were created last, after God said 'Let us make humankind in our image' (Genesis 1:26). Only humans have a rational soul and can know and love God, so they are called to relationship with God and with each other (2nd mark).

Source of authority: In Laudato Si' (2015), Pope Francis teaches that 'dominion' in Genesis 1:28 does not justify exploitation. He calls Catholics to an 'ecological conversion' to care for 'our common home'. This applies the belief in stewardship directly, so Catholics today should reduce waste and act on climate change (2 marks).
questions.examTip: A papal encyclical is a valid 'source of Christian belief and teaching'. Give its name and apply what it says to the question.

questions.question:
Explain two things that the Genesis creation accounts teach Catholics about God.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: God is omnipotent and transcendent (1 mark). In Genesis 1 God creates simply by speaking: 'Let there be light'. He exists before and beyond everything he creates, which Catholics express as creation ex nihilo, out of nothing (CCC 296) (2nd mark).

Second teaching: God is personal, loving and immanent (1 mark). In Genesis 2 God shapes the man from dust and 'breathed into his nostrils the breath of life' (Genesis 2:7). He provides a garden and a companion, which shows that God is closely involved with his creation and cares for human needs (2nd mark).

Source of authority: Genesis 1:31 says 'God saw everything that he had made, and indeed, it was very good'. This teaches that God is good and that the material world is not evil. Catholics therefore see creation as a gift to be valued and cared for (2 marks).
questions.examTip: Precise quotations from Genesis are easy evidence to learn. Short phrases are enough.

questions.question:
'The Genesis creation stories cannot be true if science explains the origin of the universe.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Scientific evidence suggests the universe began around 13.8 billion years ago in the Big Bang, and that life developed over billions of years through evolution by natural selection. Genesis 1 describes the world being made in six days, with plants appearing before the sun. If Genesis is read as a factual account, it clashes with what science has found.

Some atheists, such as Richard Dawkins, argue that once science gives a complete natural explanation, there is no need for God. On this view, the creation stories are pre-scientific myths and so are not 'true'.

Some Christians agree that the two cannot both be right, but they reject the science. Young Earth creationists believe the Bible is inerrant and must be literally true, so they reject evolution and an ancient universe. Both they and many atheists assume that the Bible and science are rivals.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

The Catholic Church teaches that there is no real conflict, because science and Genesis answer different questions. Science explains how the universe developed. Genesis explains who created it and why. The Catechism says Genesis expresses the truth of creation in 'figurative language' (CCC 390). The truths it teaches are that God is creator, that creation is good and that humans have dignity, and none of these is contradicted by physics or biology.

Catholic tradition values science. The Big Bang theory was first proposed by Fr Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest. Pope John Paul II said in 1996 that evolution is 'more than a hypothesis'. The Pontifical Academy of Sciences includes leading scientists. Pope Pius XII (Humani Generis, 1950) allowed Catholics to accept evolution of the body, provided they believe God directly creates each human soul.

Science may even point towards God. Some argue that the Big Bang raises the question of what caused it, which links to the cosmological argument (Aquinas's 'first cause'). The fine-tuning of the universe for life suggests design. On this view, science describes the method God used.

A story can also be 'true' without being literal, in the way a parable is true. Genesis teaches that the world is ordered, good and created in love, and that humans are stewards (Genesis 2:15). These are truths about meaning and purpose that science cannot test.

CONCLUSION

The statement only works if Genesis is understood as a scientific report. If it is read literally, there is a genuine conflict. But the Catholic Church does not read it that way. It sees faith and reason as 'two wings' (John Paul II, Fides et Ratio). Since science explains processes while Genesis explains meaning and purpose, the more convincing conclusion is that Genesis can be true in the ways that matter most, even if science explains how the universe began.
evidence: John Paul II, 1996 address on evolution; Fides et Ratio (1998)
questions.examTip: Avoid presenting this as 'religion versus science'. The best answers show that Christians themselves disagree (literalist versus Catholic) and explain why.

questions.question:
'Humans have a duty to protect the environment above everything else.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Genesis teaches that God placed humans in the garden 'to till it and keep it' (Genesis 2:15). Humans are therefore stewards who must answer to God for how they treat creation. If the earth is damaged beyond repair by climate change, pollution and loss of species, every other human activity is threatened. Some would say protecting it must come first.

Pope Francis's Laudato Si' (2015) speaks of an urgent ecological crisis. It warns that the earth 'is beginning to look more and more like an immense pile of filth'. It calls all people to 'ecological conversion'. The Catechism says humans may not use animals and nature without regard for the 'integrity of creation' (CCC 2415). Since the poorest people suffer most from environmental damage, protecting the environment is also a matter of justice.

Many non-religious people, including environmental activists, argue that the survival of the planet is the most basic priority. They see humans as part of nature, not above it.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

Catholic teaching does not put the environment 'above everything else'. Humans alone are made 'in the image of God' (Genesis 1:27), so human life and dignity have a unique value. Laudato Si' rejects a 'biocentrism' that treats humans as just one species among many. It teaches 'integral ecology': care for nature must go together with care for the poor, the unborn and the vulnerable. Protecting the environment while ignoring human suffering would be a distortion.

The greatest commandment is to love God, and the second is to love one's neighbour (Matthew 22:37–39). For a Catholic, the first duty is to God. Caring for creation is one way of loving God and neighbour, not something higher than them. Treating nature as the highest value could even become a form of idolatry.

There are also practical trade-offs. Poor communities may need development, such as roads, electricity and farming, to escape poverty. Catholic agencies such as CAFOD try to balance sustainability with people's right to a decent life (Gaudium et Spes 26).

CONCLUSION

The statement is right that care for creation is a serious, God-given duty and that the environmental crisis is urgent. But the words 'above everything else' go too far from a Catholic perspective. The most convincing view is that environmental protection is part of a wider duty: to love God, respect human dignity and seek the common good. As Laudato Si' puts it, 'everything is connected'. Humans should protect the environment as an expression of love for God and neighbour, not instead of it.
evidence: Laudato Si' (2015): ecological conversion, integral ecology
questions.examTip: Words like 'above everything else' are what you are being asked to judge. Make sure your conclusion addresses them directly.
